publication_scope.blurb: Ludwig Crocius — Book II Chapter 4 On the immortality of the soul from clear testimonies of Scripture, from the 1636 Bremen Latin. Densify COMPLETE (mid PHYS 354–mid-356): Cap. 4 title; OT/NT testimonies; Ecclesiastes 12:7 (Augustine); Matthew 10:28; Lazarus; thief on the cross; Philippians 1:23; Stephen; Revelation 6:9 — Cap. 4 close. Cap. 5 starts mid PHYS 356 (De statu animae a corpore separata). Liber I Cap.1–11 and Liber II Cap.1–3 COMPLETE (english not modified).

source_text: CAPUT QUARTUM, De animae immortalitate e perspicuis scripturae testimoniis. Hactenus fuerunt authoritates & rationes de animae immortalitate: sequuntur perspicua scripturarum testimonia, quibus ea Christianis omninoque scripturas recipientibus demonstratur. II. Sunt autem illa V. aut N. T.
english: CHAPTER FOUR. On the immortality of the soul from clear testimonies of Scripture.

Hitherto there have been authorities and reasons concerning the immortality of the soul: there follow clear testimonies of the Scriptures, by which it is demonstrated to Christians and to all who receive the Scriptures.
II. And those testimonies are of the Old or of the New Testament.

source_text: Sic Paulus Phil. 1.v.23. dimitti desiderat, & esse cum Christo. Sic Stephanus protomartyr lapidatus, jamque moriturus, Domine Jesu, inquit, recipe Spiritum meum, Act. 7.v.59. Sic Johannes Apoc. 6.v.9. videt sub altari animas eorum, qui mactati propter verbum Dei.
english: So Paul in Philippians 1:23 desires to depart and to be with Christ. So Stephen the first martyr, stoned and now about to die, says, Lord Jesus, receive my Spirit (Acts 7:59). So John in Revelation 6:9 sees under the altar the souls of those who were slain for the word of God.

source_text: III. In V. T. maxime perspicuum est illud Eccles. 12.v.7. redibit pulver (corpus e pulvere productum) in terram, quemadmodum fuit, (e terra factum in terram reverti oportet) spiritus autem redibit ad Deum, qui dedit ipsum. Hic opponuntur corpus & spiritus sive anima rationalis: & sicut sunt diversae naturae atque originis, ita & diversum exitum sortiuntur. Corpus quidem ex humo & materia factum, in hoc ipsum, ex quo factum, redit sive resolvitur, i.e. interit. Anima vero non ex aliqua materia, sed e nihilo producta, cum redit, non habet, quo redeat, nisi ad autorem, qui eam dedit, ut scribit Augustinus lib. 10. de Genesi ad literam.
english: III. In the Old Testament that of Ecclesiastes 12:7 is most clear: the dust (the body produced from dust) will return to the earth as it was (what was made from earth ought to return into earth), but the spirit will return to God who gave it. Here body and spirit or the rational soul are opposed: and as they are of diverse nature and origin, so also they obtain a diverse exit. The body indeed, made from soil and matter, returns or is resolved into that very thing from which it was made — that is, it perishes. But the soul, produced not from any matter but from nothing, when it returns has nowhere to return except to the author who gave it, as Augustine writes in On Genesis Literally book 10.

source_text: IV. In N. T. Christus immortalitatem animae & a corpore diversam naturam asserit clarissime Matth. 10.v.28. nolite metuere ab iis, qui interimunt corpus, animam autem non possunt interimere. Si anima rationalis esset mortalis, & ejusdem cum corpore conditionis, cur interimi non posset, sicut corpus interimitur? Sic etiam narratio Servatoris de epulone & Lazaro, morte corporis haud finiri omnia, clare ostendit Luc. 16.v.22. & seqq. Sic in cruce pro humano genere mortem jam oppetitorus latroni poenitenti mox animam acturo sancte affirmat, Hodie mecum eris in paradiso, Luc. 23.v.43. corpore sane non nisi in cruce ac sepulchro, anima vero cum Christo in Paradiso.
english: IV. In the New Testament Christ most clearly asserts the immortality of the soul and a nature diverse from the body (Matthew 10:28): do not fear those who kill the body, but cannot kill the soul. If the rational soul were mortal and of the same condition with the body, why could it not be killed as the body is killed? So also the Savior's narrative of the rich man and Lazarus clearly shows that by the death of the body all things are not finished (Luke 16:22 and following). So on the cross, about to meet death for the human race, he solemnly affirms to the penitent thief who was about to act out his soul, Today you will be with me in paradise (Luke 23:43) — with the body indeed nowhere but on the cross and in the tomb, but with the soul with Christ in Paradise.
